description: We are CosOrbit—a trio of students, united by our love for STEM and space exploration. Our goal is to encourage young learners about exploration in outer space, combining creative problem-solving with actual scientific NASA data to build innovative and impactful solutions. With that, we hope to inspire and train future generations of junior astronauts by making science fun and accessible.
summary: CosOrbit: Junior Space Academy is an interactive browser game where students (ages 7–12) transform passive space learning into hands-on mission command. Player manages a lunar or Martian outpost, balancing four vital resources (power, life support, radiation shielding, and health) while responding to solar storms, dust storms or equipment leaks. Every decision carries a cost while completing minigames to survive. CosOrbit addresses the challenge by simulating authentic operational pressures—grounded in real telemetry including solar flares and geomagnetic storm alerts from NASA’s DONKI database and the NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, radiation doses scale from the Curiosity rover’s RAD instrument, solar power follows NASA’s Mars sunlight data and oxygen production draws from the Perseverance MOXIE experiment. Our system translates these parameters into visual warning levels and dynamic emergencies. Every choice carries a trade-off such as  burying the habitat for shielding at the cost of solar power or rationing oxygen during blackouts. It is important as it bridges scientific authenticity with educational accessibility while teaching students resource management and crisis response through active gameplay rather than memorization. Featuring zero installation requirements, multi-difficulty progression and an engaging classroom-friendly tool that inspires the next generation of space explorers.
details:
CosOrbit: Junior Space Academy is an interactive, browser-based space outpost simulation and educational game built for students (ages 7 to 12) and beginner space enthusiasts.

What it does and how it works

  • ​Players manage a 6-person student/astronaut crew living on a lunar or Martian base across multiple days (Sols). Before launch, the player picks a difficulty (Rookie, Pilot or Commander), an objective and a real NASA landing site.
  • There are 12 sites in total such as Jezero Crater, Gale Crater and Tranquility Base. The player can also visit real landing sites, each with simplified buffs and debuffs inspired by its actual features, and a tutorial and a glossary (sol, mSv, regolith) explain the terms.
  • Each site gives a bonus and a penalty drawn from its real features. The player also designs the crew.
  • Each day involves a strategic decision and resource management (Power, Life Support, Radiation Shielding and Crew Health).
  • The player reads a forecast, makes one choice at Mission Control and plays a mini-game such as sheltering from a solar storm, fixing an air leak, cleaning dust off solar panels, driving a rover or doing an airlock safety check.
  • Four meters (power, life support, shield and health) show the cost of every choice. Each mission ends with a rocket launch and a capsule landing that re-entry mirrors Artemis II flight profiles.
  • A hidden Odyssey mission, based on NASA's real Mars plans (about 24 sols) unlocks for players who earn three stars on all three levels (Rookie, Pilot and Commander). Odyssey has every mini-game, a random site and a mission as long as a real NASA one.

Benefits

  • The game teaches children and students aged 7 to 12 authentic concepts in space science, astronomy, and astronaut safety operations (e.g. radiation units, solar weather, radio signal delays, and life support systems).
  • Students learn real space ideas by making trade-offs about radiation, power, air and the radio delay to Earth. "Real NASA science" panel lists each number with its source and says which values are simplified.
  • A “Space words” tutorial page explains terms like mSv, sol, regolith and X-class flare, so young players aren’t stopped by jargon.
  • The end screen links the crew's radiation dose to days on the space station and has discussion questions for teachers.
  • The game is a single HTML file. It runs in any browser on phones, tablets and computers with no installation, uses touch or keyboard, saves progress and 25 achievements in the browser.

Intended impact

The goal is to make space science feel personal and to show students 7 to 12 years old that space missions are about careful planning and trade-offs, not only rockets. Students name their crew, protect them and see why radiation is one of the biggest barriers to human spaceflight. The game aims to spark curiosity about careers in space and give classrooms a starting point for discussing real NASA data.

Tools and technology

​Vanilla HTML5, CSS3 (with responsive custom grid/flex layouts) and modern JavaScript (ES6+ APIs, HTML5 Canvas 2D graphics, Web Audio API for procedural sound effects and music) with no external libraries or network calls.

All characters, bases, planets and effects are drawn in code, and the mini-games run on requestAnimationFrame loops.

Music and sound effects are generated live with the Web Audio API, so there are no audio files.

Saved progress and achievements use localStorage. It works on phones, with swipe-sideways crew design and touch controls.

Quality checks: The page uses screen-reader labels and respects reduced-motion settings.

​Hardware/Software: Developed using a personally owned student laptop and standard web browsers (Chrome/Firefox/Safari) without requiring external heavy software engines or server installations. Others coding and development tools used are Claude, ElevenLabs, Gemini and Netlify.

What makes it creative

  • It’s an honest simulation of trade-offs rather than a quiz with a space theme. Real radiation numbers drive the difficulty. Every choice has a cost, so there is no free move, as in real mission planning.
  • Each landing site's bonus and penalty come from its real features, for example Hellas Planitia's deep basin lowers radiation and Malapert Massif has good radio contact with Earth.
  • Players see their astronauts running around the base, fixing parts and chatting with each other.
  • There are more than 20 distinct mini-games that Moon and Mars play differently (a 14-day lunar night shortened to 3 for pacing or Mars dust storms and weak sunlight).
  • Everything, including art, music and effects, is code-generated, which keeps the whole thing tiny and shareable.
  • The Malaysian-flag rocket and the Sarawak Space Challenge link give it a local identity.

Factors the team considered

Scientific accuracy: The science panel lists sources for each figure. Examples include Curiosity’s RAD instrument (about 0.64–0.7 mSv/day on Mars, 1.8–1.9 on the trip there), the space station’s 0.4–1.0 mSv/day, and the May 2024 X8.7 flare. It also says plainly that game effects are simplified.

Transparency about data: A hosted page can’t call NASA’s servers, so values were copied by hand into a saved snapshot and the game says so. It links to NOAA SWPC and NASA DONKI for today’s real space weather.

Age-appropriateness: Short text, bright visuals, a tutorial and the glossary page for hard words.

Accessibility: The game works on phones and computers that needs no installation or account. It has controls for keyboard and touch, plus music and sound toggles

Fair difficulty: Three levels (rookie, pilot and commander), a forecast shown every day, and tips on the final tutorial page.

Replay value: More sites, mini-games and achievements, plus a secret mode that give players reasons to come back.
